x-flow.title: Job flow
x-flow.intro: Jobs run asynchronously: submitting a query returns immediately with an `execution_id`, and the query keeps running in the background until you poll it to completion.

steps.note: Repeat on an interval until `status` is no longer in progress

notes: **Poll `status`, not `results`.** `GET .../status` is cheap and returns `results_url` once the job is done; `GET .../results` is what actually pages through the data, `num_rows`/`offset` at a time, following `next_page` for more.

**`results` and `download` are independent, not exclusive.** Pull a page inline with `results` to inspect it in your app, or stream the whole set with `download` as CSV, newline-delimited JSON, or Parquet — call either, neither, or both once the job has finished.

post.description: Submit a SQL job for execution. `:name` placeholders in sql_text are resolved from the parameters field, falling back to the caller's saved variables for anything not passed explicitly - see parameters below and the Variables API.

post.summary: Save job results to a dataset
post.description: Copy the results of a completed job into a new dataset, so they outlive the job's retention window. The dataset must not already exist.

get.description: Retrieve the execution status of a previously submitted job.

Retrieve the results of a previously submitted job. While the job is still running the response is 202 with its status. Pass `wait` (seconds, up to 20) to have the request held until the job's status changes, so a client can poll this one endpoint instead of /status followed by /results. Pass `seen` (the status the client last saw) so a change that happened before the request arrived is answered at once rather than missed.
Download the results of a previously submitted job as CSV, newline-delimited JSON, or Parquet.

schema.title: Response Get Recent User Queries Api V1 Jobs Recent Get

get.summary: List trigger-fired runs for one step
get.description: Run history for standing work. Lists the jobs a trigger has fired for one target object, or for one source dataset, most recent first. Ask by either `target` (the view or task the run works on) or `dataset` (the dataset carrying the trigger, optionally narrowed to one `trigger` name) - exactly one of the two. Visible to anyone who may READ the object, which is the same grant that shows the trigger in `information_schema.triggers`; a fired run's own `submitted_by` is the trigger's runs-as identity, so ownership is not the question here. `status` is the JOB's status - whether THIS RUN succeeded - which is a different thing from the trigger's `last_fired_status` (whether the fire happened) and from the target view's `LastRefreshStatus` (whether the latest work succeeded). A fire that was refused - suspended, egress-blocked, owner-missing - or deduplicated into another job never became a job and so never appears here: an empty list is not evidence that nothing happened. History reaches back at most `retention_days`, after which the documents are purged. `limit` is optional: omitted, the listing runs to the 1000-row ceiling, which within the retention window is usually the whole history.

schema.title: Response List Fired Runs Api V1 Jobs Fired Get

get.description: List the caller's saved query-parameter variables.

put.summary: Create or update a saved variable
put.description: Create (or replace) a named query-parameter variable for the caller.

delete.description: Delete a named query-parameter variable for the caller.

post.summary: Check a SQL statement without running it
post.description: Resolve and type-check one statement against the catalog, as the caller, and report what was found: a positioned error to underline, the result shape, and the relations and columns in scope for completion. Reads no data and changes nothing, so it is safe to call as a statement is typed. A statement that is wrong is a 200 with `ok: false` - the error is the answer, not a failure of the request.

post.summary: Estimate how much data a SQL statement would process
post.description: Plan one statement as the caller, without running it, and report the bytes processed it would be billed for - the same plan-time figure the run bills - with a rough duration and, for a payer with a daily allowance, how much of today's allowance it would use. Heavier than `/check`: planning reads manifests and statistics, so call it once a statement checks out and typing has paused, not on every keystroke. A statement that is wrong is a 200 with `ok: false`.

get.summary: Today's usage against the daily allowance
get.description: The caller's billing account (or, without one, the caller), its effective plan, and - when that plan has a daily allowance - today's and this month's bytes processed, as counted for enforcement.

CheckedColumn.title: CheckedColumn
CheckedColumn.description:
One column, as the check resolved it.

`type` is the canonical SQL spelling — the same text a stored schema persists and
`SHOW COLUMNS` prints, so an editor showing it beside a completion is showing
something the reader can also type.

source.title: Source
source.description: For a column, the relation qualifying it; None if computed here

data_type.title: Data Type
data_type.description: The column's SQL type; None for relations

CheckedIdentity.title: CheckedIdentity
CheckedIdentity.description:
One name the statement makes available, and what it stands for.

This is the completion vocabulary: after `FROM sales.orders AS o`, `o` is a name
the reader can type; after `COUNT(*) AS n`, so is `n`.

CheckedRelation.title: CheckedRelation
CheckedRelation.description:
A relation in scope, under the name the statement refers to it by.

`alias` is what qualifies a column here (`p` in `FROM $planets AS p`); `relation`
is what it actually is. `columns` is the FULL column list, not just the ones the
statement referenced — completion needs the ones it did not.

constraint.title: Constraint
constraint.description: The handle `DROP CONSTRAINT` removes it by

kind.title: Kind
kind.description: Always `maps` today - the only kind that is a join

cardinality_observed.title: Cardinality Observed
cardinality_observed.description: What verification last measured, which may contradict the declaration. A `many_to_one` that is really many-to-many is a fan-out that inflates every number computed through the join. None where it has not been measured

origin.title: Origin
origin.description: `asserted` - a person declared it - or `inferred`, a machine's proposal

verified_at.title: Verified At
verified_at.description: When the values were last checked against each other, UTC ISO-8601. None means never checked, which is a state rather than a default

CheckedRelationship.title: CheckedRelationship
CheckedRelationship.description:
A declared correspondence between two columns, for the editor to offer as
a join predicate the reader edits before running.

Flat, not nested under an entry in `relations`: a relationship is an object
about TWO datasets, so hanging it off one of them forces a choice about
which, or duplicates it under both. The consumer's question - what connects
these two aliases - is a lookup over pairs.

Oriented as stored, referencing -> referenced, and each relationship appears
once. Orientation is information (it is what `m.planet_id = p.id` is read
off) rather than something the reader has to normalise away.

NOT ENFORCED, ever. Nothing validated this when it was declared and nothing
validates it now; a row on either side with no match on the other is
perfectly legal. This says someone wrote the correspondence down, never that
the data honours it.

bytes_processed.title: Bytes Processed
bytes_processed.description: Bytes processed per UTC day (1 GB = 10^9 bytes); null if not capped

ErrorPosition.title: ErrorPosition
ErrorPosition.description:
Where in the submitted SQL a failure is, for the editor to underline.

A half-open range, in both conventions the editor might want, so the client does
no arithmetic: 1-based `line`/`column` (what Monaco's IRange takes) and 0-based
`offset` (what a plain string slice takes). They describe the same span.

Coordinates index the SQL exactly as the caller submitted it — comments, line
breaks and all — not any normalised form of it.

bytes_allowance.title: Bytes Allowance
bytes_allowance.description: Bytes processed allowed per UTC day

bytes_used.title: Bytes Used
bytes_used.description: Bytes already settled against today's allowance

bytes_remaining.title: Bytes Remaining
bytes_remaining.description: Allowance left before this statement, never negative

fits.title: Fits
fits.description: Whether running this statement stays within what is left

EstimateAllowance.title: EstimateAllowance
EstimateAllowance.description: Where this statement leaves a capped (free-plan) payer's data allowance today.

sql_text.title: Sql Text
sql_text.description: SQL statement to execute. Required unless `throttled` is set - a throttled fire never built one to run.

throttled.title: Throttled
throttled.description: Records that a trigger reached this fire but was deliberately suppressed by its own minimum-interval floor, rather than submitting SQL for execution. No statement is parsed or run, no worker is dispatched, and nobody is billed: a job document is written directly with a terminal `THROTTLED` status, so the fire still has a row in the same run history a real firing would. `client_info.trigger` carries the provenance (workspace, target, trigger name) in place of the statement jobs would otherwise have derived it from. Only the platform's own trigger-firing identity may set this, on the same terms as unattended trigger provenance generally.

parameters.title: Parameters
parameters.description: Values for any `:name` placeholders in sql_text, as key-value pairs. Values passed here always take priority. Any placeholder the query references that isn't included here is automatically resolved from the caller's saved variables (see the Variables API) - this is what lets a shared query stay generic (e.g. `WHERE department = :department`) while each caller's own saved value fills in without them passing it explicitly. A placeholder that's neither passed nor saved is left unresolved, and the job fails at execution with a parameter-not-defined error. Each value is typed: `{"type": "<canonical type>", "value": ...}`, e.g. `{"type": "DATE", "value": "2026-01-01"}` or `{"type": "INT64", "value": 42}`. The engine binds it as `CAST(value AS type)`, so `type` is a canonical type name (VARCHAR, INT64, FLOAT64, DECIMAL(p,s), BOOL, DATE, TIMESTAMP, ...) and `value` is a string, number, boolean or null. A bare value is refused.

example.sql_text: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 10

QueryCheckError.title: QueryCheckError
QueryCheckError.description:
What the check found wrong, in the shape the editor draws.

`position` is absent for a failure with nowhere in the statement to point — a
permission refusal is about the relation, not about a place in the text — and for
one the engine recorded no span for. It is never synthesised: a made-up range
marks the wrong text, which is worse than marking none.

sql_text.title: Sql Text
sql_text.description: One SQL statement to check. Not a batch.

parameters.title: Parameters
parameters.description: Values for the statement's `:name` placeholders. Anything not passed is resolved from the caller's saved variables, exactly as job submission resolves them - see the Variables API. Each value is typed: `{"type": "<canonical type>", "value": ...}`, e.g. `{"type": "DATE", "value": "2026-01-01"}` or `{"type": "INT64", "value": 42}`. The engine binds it as `CAST(value AS type)`, so `type` is a canonical type name (VARCHAR, INT64, FLOAT64, DECIMAL(p,s), BOOL, DATE, TIMESTAMP, ...) and `value` is a string, number, boolean or null. A bare value is refused.

ok.title: Ok
ok.description: Nothing was found wrong. `error` is set exactly when false

columns.title: Columns
columns.description: The result shape. Empty for a statement returning no rows, and for one that did not check out

relations.title: Relations
relations.description: Every relation read, at full width. Present as far as the binder got, even on failure

identities.title: Identities
identities.description: Every name the statement makes available. Also survives a failed bind, partially

relationships.title: Relationships
relationships.description: Declared relationships with at least one end among the relations resolved, for offering a join predicate. Both ends of every entry are readable by the caller. Includes edges whose far end is NOT in the statement yet - that is how the editor knows about a table one keystroke before it binds

writes.title: Writes
writes.description: The subset of `tables` whose contents the statement writes, sorted

parameters.title: Parameters
parameters.description: The `:name` placeholders needed, no leading colon

QueryCheckResponse.title: QueryCheckResponse
QueryCheckResponse.description:
What a check found. A statement being wrong is a 200 with `ok: false`.

Fields mirror `opteryx.planner.query_check.QueryCheck` one-for-one; see
`tests/test_query_check.py`, which fails if the engine grows a field this drops.

ok.title: Ok
ok.description: The statement planned. `error` is set exactly when false

estimated.title: Estimated
estimated.description: Whether a figure was produced. False for a statement that did not plan, and for DDL, which is not planned here

billing_bytes.title: Billing Bytes
billing_bytes.description: Bytes processed this statement will be billed for if run now - the same plan-time figure the run bills, not an approximation of it. Can change if a relation it reads is committed to before it runs

estimated_time_bin.title: Estimated Time Bin
estimated_time_bin.description: Rough duration: `<1s`, `1-5s`, `5-15s` or `>15s`. Read as 'at least this slow'

cached.title: Cached
cached.description: Served from a recent identical estimate

allowance.description: Only for a free-plan payer with a daily data allowance, and omitted if usage could not be read - an estimate is still useful without it

QueryEstimateResponse.title: QueryEstimateResponse
QueryEstimateResponse.description: The bytes running a statement now would process. A wrong statement is a 200 with `ok: false`.

QueryJob.title: QueryJob
QueryJob.description:
Pydantic model for a user-facing Firestore job document.

Only the specified subset of attributes are represented here - Firestore
documents include additional fields that are intentionally ignored.

Fields marked as "optional" are only present when the query is complete.
The model accepts Firestore Timestamp-like objects (with ``to_datetime``)
and will coerce them to Python ``datetime`` objects.

RelationshipEnd.title: RelationshipEnd
RelationshipEnd.description:
One end of a relationship, as split parts.

Never a dotted string: a dataset name may contain dots, so a consumer handed
`"public.astronomy.moons"` has to decide where the boundaries are, and the
consumers that already do it disagree with each other. Split once, here.

dataset.title: Dataset
dataset.description: Name of the dataset to create

workspace.title: Workspace
workspace.description: Workspace to create the dataset in. Defaults to `personal`, which is where a caller always has rights to their own collection.

collection.title: Collection
collection.description: Collection within the workspace. Defaults to the caller's own username, giving `personal.{username}.{dataset}` - the one target that needs no granted policy.

SaveJobRequest.title: SaveJobRequest
SaveJobRequest.description:
Where to save a completed job's results.

The source job is NOT here: it is the `{identifier}` path segment, so it is
authorised by the same code that guards `/results` and `/download` rather
than arriving as a body field that a caller can point anywhere.

execution_id.title: Execution Id
execution_id.description: Id of the SAVE job, not of the source job

source_execution_id.title: Source Execution Id
source_execution_id.description: The job whose results are being saved

status.title: Status
status.description: Current state of the save job

plan.title: Plan
plan.description: The effective plan: free, prepaid, payg or house

metered.title: Metered
metered.description: Whether this account has a daily allowance that blocks when used

VariableInfo.title: VariableInfo
VariableInfo.description: A single saved query-parameter variable, as returned to the caller.

type.title: Type
type.description: A canonical type name, e.g. VARCHAR, INT64, FLOAT64, BOOL, DATE

value.title: Value
value.description: The variable's value; it must CAST to `type` exactly as a typed parameter would
